one_liner: C++11 SIMD vector types (float_v, double_v) with vectorized math for x86 SSE2-AVX2; beats per-element scalar <cmath> loops.
what_it_does: Vc gives explicitly data-parallel value types (Vc::float_v, Vc::double_v, masks, SimdArray and simdize helpers) whose width follows the target ISA, so code written once compiles to SSE2, AVX or AVX2 instructions. You restructure loops to operate on whole vectors, use masked assignment (y(mask) = ...) for branches, and call vectorized math such as Vc::exp, Vc::log and Vc::sqrt. It is not a drop-in for <cmath>: the interface is a new type system, built from headers plus a small static library (libVc.a).
how_it_is_fast: Each operation maps to one SIMD instruction over 4 doubles (AVX/AVX2) or 2 (SSE), and data-dependent control flow becomes mask arithmetic instead of per-element branches. The transcendental functions are vectorized Cephes-style range reduction plus polynomial evaluation (exp via 2^n scaling and a degree-6 polynomial), so one call evaluates a whole vector instead of one libm call per element.
when_to_use: Existing x86-only C++ code that needs explicit SIMD across SSE2 to AVX2 without writing intrinsics, especially loops that span function or translation-unit boundaries where auto-vectorization fails.

Element-wise transcendental work on double or float arrays (exp, log, sqrt over thousands of values): in the Euro-Par 2016 logs Vc's width-4 kernels ran 1.8-4.4x faster than per-element std::exp/std::log/std::sqrt on Haswell.
Branchy per-element kernels (conditional calls, early returns) that can be expressed as masks: 2.3-5.1x on the conditional_math_call and early_return kernels of the same study.
Toolchains stuck at C++11 or C++14 (GCC 4.8.1+, clang 3.4+), where std::experimental::simd is not available.
when_not_to_use: New projects: the README says Vc is in maintenance mode and no longer actively developed, and points users to std-simd (std::experimental::simd, shipped with GCC 11 libstdc++).

AVX-512, ARM NEON/SVE, RISC-V or GPUs: the README lists only SSE2 to AVX2 (AVX-512 and NEON struck out, MIC removed in 1.4); other targets fall back to the Scalar implementation with vector width 1, so no speedup.
Loops with lane-divergent trip counts: the while_loop SQRT kernel ran at 0.78x of the scalar reference (59.7 vs 46.6 ns per element), because masked-off lanes keep iterating.
When hand-tuned intrinsics are acceptable: manual AVX2 code beat the Vc version in 12 of 15 single-thread cases in the same logs (for example simple EXP 6.18 vs 7.86 ns per element).

integration.dependencies: none at runtime; CMake 3.5+ to build libVc.a (git submodules only for the test tree)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; GCC 4.8.1+, clang 3.4+, ICC 18.0.5+, Visual Studio 2019 (64-bit target)
integration.platforms: x86 and x86-64 with SSE2, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1/4.2, SSE4a, AVX, AVX2 (+FMA, FMA4, XOP, BMI2); everything else compiles to the Scalar implementation (width 1)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; vectors are plain value types with no shared state

gotchas: Vector width and therefore data layout and function signatures follow the compile flags (Vc_IMPL is chosen from __AVX2__, __AVX__, __SSE4_2__ and so on), so every translation unit and libVc.a must target the same ISA; a static constructor in every TU calls checkLibraryAbi at startup and aborts if headers and library disagree.
Containers of Vc types need over-aligned allocation: std::vector<double_v> or structs holding Vc vectors should use Vc::Allocator or Vc_DECLARE_ALLOCATOR, as the Vc/Allocator header documents.

Masked operations still compute every lane: in the benchmark y(mask) = Vc::exp(...) evaluated all 4 lanes and masked only the store, while the scalar reference skipped about half of the calls (50% random mask) but paid a data-dependent branch; speedups therefore depend on mask density. Results matched the reference to about 3e-16 (exp) and 3e-15 (log) relative error, but the functions are polynomial approximations, not correctly rounded (the float exp returns 0 below about -88.03 instead of a subnormal).

Open bugs remain: #349 (SSE uchar min/max built with schar; a September 2023 commit 'Fix horizontal max/min for uchar' may cover it), #257 (wrong short SimdArray division), #249 (macOS upper AVX register halves), #242 (clang 7 miscompiled AVX/AVX2 on the 1.3 branch) and #367 (Xcode 26 beta build error, with a C++23 missing-include fix committed in April 2026).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued siblings, xsimd is the comparable SIMD-type wrapper, while SLEEF, VDT and fmath only supply vectorized math functions; pick Vc when you maintain x86 code already written against Vc 1.x, or need its masked-assignment and simdize API on a C++11 compiler, and otherwise prefer xsimd or std::experimental::simd for new code and SLEEF or VDT when you only need vector exp/log/sin.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party Euro-Par 2016 data (Wende et al., flwende/simd_benchmarks): one thread on a Xeon E5-2680v3 (Haswell) pinned at 1.9 GHz, GCC 5.3.0 -O3 -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma, 8192 doubles with a 50% random call mask; Vc 1.2.0 double_v kernels against a per-element, out-of-line scalar loop over std::exp/std::log/std::sqrt (libstdc++ to glibc) ran 1.34-5.07x faster in 14 of 15 kernel and function pairs and 0.78x on while_loop SQRT. The logs print the max relative error against the reference (3.5e-16 for simple EXP, 3.2e-15 for simple LOG, 0 for while_loop SQRT), so the outputs were checked; the baseline was deliberately non-vectorizable, so no comparison with auto-vectorized code exists.
status_note: Maintenance mode by the authors' own statement, but the 1.4 branch still takes compatibility and CI fixes (C++23 includes in April 2026, a GCC 14 CMake fix in July 2026; last release 1.4.5 in June 2024; 80 open issues); BSD-3-Clause and easy to build, best kept for existing x86 Vc users.
